body:
# Suttungr: canonical, contested, and the false forms on record

*A letter to a colleague, 31 July 2026 — on the name Suttungr, and on the forms that keep failing it.*

Your note said, roughly: surely the marks are a nicety. Permit me to use Suttungr to show they are not.

First, the attestation. The attested form is **ᛋᚢᛏᛏᚢᚾᚴᚱ**, from the tradition's own record. The canonical transliteration is **Suttungr**.

Say it aloud as the sources heard it: 'SOOT-toongr' — two beats, the first stressed, the double t held a fraction long in the middle, and the final -r trilled as a syllable of its own, as in Icelandic Suttungur. The marks are what carry that sound to a reader who has never heard it spoken.

On the plain form — and I want to be precise, because you pushed on this. The plain form *suttungr* differs from the canonical *Suttungr* only by convention of display — case, not content. It is *acceptable everywhere*: in legacy systems, in plain-text citation, in the DNS itself. What is not acceptable is what follows in the register: respellings that change the letters, not just their case.

One more thing, because it always surprises: the name did not stay home. Suttungr's closest kin are inside the corpus itself.  The mead myth belongs to the great northern pattern of the coveted treasure prised from giant-keepers: Þórr winning the mile-wide brewing cauldron from Hymir so that Ægir can brew for the gods is the same plot in beer rather than poetry, and Lindow reads the two tales as sibling statements about how culture's goods are obtained — never made at home, always taken across the boundary.

And it never stopped working. Suttungr's afterlife is the afterlife of the mead itself: every retelling of Norse poetry's origin, from the Kearys' Victorian 'Heroes of Asgard' onward, replays the auger-hole, the golden seat, and the two eagles over the wall of Ásgarðr.  The romantics loved Gunnlöð and made Suttungr a brooding proprietor; the skaldic scholars made him something rarer, a mnemonic fixed point — because 'Suttungr's mead' stayed a living kenning, his name travelled inside every stanza that called verse by its owner's title.

## The Convention's Own History

The Poetic Edda survives essentially in one manuscript — the Codex Regius, c. 1270 — and normalized Old Norse spelling descends from what that manuscript and its siblings actually write. Þ and ð are not decorations: they are letters of the alphabet the skalds used (and English later abandoned), and ǫ is a nasal vowel the normalization preserves because the sources carry it. The register's rule is the manuscript's rule: spell the names the way the tradition that sang them wrote them down.

## Where Protocol Meets Practice

The technical answer is simple: the canonical marks are legal IDNA 2008 characters, encoded as punycode under `xn--`. The practical answer is messier: legal does not mean stocked (registrar inventory is partial), and stocked does not mean typeable (stacked diacritics defeat mobile keyboards).

So the register's rule is a hierarchy of attested forms — full restoration, circumflex, macron-only, attested variant, and finally plain ASCII for the systems that cannot carry marks. Every rung is defensible because every rung is attested. The forms this register rules against are not rungs; they are errors, and errors do not get rungs.

Write back when you have checked the sources; they are better company than I am.

*— The Register*

## The Verdict

**Suttungr** is the canonical form: attested, checkable, and enforced across the temple, the lexicon, the cards, the APIs, and this register. The plain form *suttungr* shares that standing — the two are the same name in every system. The false forms above are documented so that no reader has to take the temple's word on faith — the violations are stated, the sources are named, and the register stands open to challenge on every line.

The temple of **Suttungr** stands at [/suttungr/](/suttungr/).

The docket for this ruling: no false forms on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 5 cited sources — Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Skáldskaparmál 3-6 (Kvasir's blood and the mead's brewing; Gillingr's death and Suttungr's ransom of the dwarfs; Hnitbjörg and Gunnlöð; Bölverkr, Baugi, and the auger Rati; the eagle chase and the rhymester's share), with the þulur (jǫtna heiti) and the kennings for poetry, Poetic Edda: Hávamál 104-110 (Óðinn's own account: Suttungr's hall, Gunnlöð's golden seat, Rati's mouth, the ring-oath, and Gunnlöð weeping) and 13-14 (the heron of forgetfulness; 'drunk I was at wise Fjalar's'), Cleasby–Vigfusson, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, s.v. suttungr; Zoëga, A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic, s.v. suttungr (name of a giant).
